blocks.title: Free probability and free cumulants
Applications: Fluctuations of random Young diagrams
blocks.content: The methods presented in this article are very useful in the study of the asymptotic properties of symmetric groups. An example of such an application is presented in our subsequent work [@Sniady2005GaussuanFluctuationsofYoungdiagrams] where we study the distribution of a random Young diagram contributing to a given reducible representation of the symmetric group $S_q$ in the limit $q\to\infty$. We prove that for a large class of such representations the fluctuations of the Young diagram around the limit shape are asymptotically Gaussian. blocks.content: In this article we manipulate with moments of the Jucys--Murphy element $J$ (or with products of such moments) and we need an efficient way to enumerate the summands in sums similar to [\[eq:wielkasuma\]](#eq:wielkasuma){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:wielkasuma"}. blocks.title: Pushing partitions
blocks.content:
In this article we are concerned mostly with conjugacy classes of permutations and not permutations themselves. For this reason we need a method to enumerate in the sums similar to [\[eq:wielkasuma\]](#eq:wielkasuma){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:wielkasuma"} not the individual summands, but whole classes of summands (summands within each class will be conjugate). Pushing partitions will turn out to be the suitable objects to enumerate such classes.

### Ramified covering and an admissible sequence

Suppose that an admissible sequence $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\{1,2,\dots,q\}$ is given. Following the idea of Okounkov [@Okounkov2000randompermutations] we consider a two--dimensional sphere ${\mathbb{S}}^2$ with distinguished points $0,1,2,\dots,n,\infty$. blocks.title: Connection with orthogonal polynomials and Wick product
blocks.content: Suppose that a probability measure $\mu$ on the real line is given. We consider a sequence $P_0,P_1,\dots$ of orthogonal polynomials with respect to the measure $\mu$. Some questions concerning these polynomials are extremely simple, for example the mean value is given by a trivial equation $\int_{\mathbb{R}}P_k(x) d\mu(x)= \delta_{0k}$, but the price for working with orthogonal polynomials is that we need a formula for expressing a product $P_k P_l$ as a linear combination of polynomials $P$ (in the non--commutative probability theory such formulas are called Wick products).
